# On Beauty and Bodily Things

I have never been good at perceiving the subtle, gentle things that others seem to feel so easily. When someone tells me the heart can sing, I picture an actual object lodged in my chest, warbling away like some trapped bird—because that is the only way I know how to make sense of it. The delicate registers of feeling escape me. I am built for the literal, and the literal rarely whispers.

This limitation, if that is what it is, has made me deeply skeptical of poetic and spiritual talk. When people begin speaking of the "Soul," I hear a grifter warming up his pitch. It sounds like a hustle, an elaborate con dressed in reverent language, designed to sell me something I can neither hold nor verify. I cannot help it. The moment the conversation drifts toward the transcendent, my guard goes up and my patience runs out.

I have tried, honestly, to lose myself in nature poetry—to let the meadows and streams and wide-open skies carry me somewhere higher. But every attempt collapses under the weight of a single, stubborn objection: I hate relieving myself outdoors. Give me a toilet and a stall, a door that latches, some measure of civilized privacy. Just as the poem reaches its swelling crescendo of wildflowers and birdsong, my mind wanders instead to the practical horror of squatting behind a bush.

And so my preoccupation with bodily functions ruins the whole enterprise. While the poet exalts the grandeur of the untamed world, I am busy imagining the labor of digging a hole, the indignity of burying my own waste, the grim arithmetic of the wilderness. The beautiful imagery dissolves, replaced by these earthbound concerns that refuse to be silenced.

Yet there is a strange consolation in all of this. I sometimes imagine what the world would look like under black-light vision—the kind that reveals what the naked eye politely ignores. Everything would glow. Every trail, every tree, every patch of ground would shine with the luminous residue of everything that has ever passed through and over it. The whole earth is coated in excrement, and under that light it would be radiant. Perhaps that is my version of beauty: not the pristine landscape the poets promise, but the filth beneath it, glowing softly, honestly, in the dark.
outputs.L4:
# On Beauty and Its Discontents

I've never been able to muster the proper reverence for nature poetry. You know the kind I mean—the sort that asks you to genuflect before a daffodil, to find God tucked into the folds of a rose petal, to hear eternity whispering in the wind through the pines. People recite these verses with their eyes half-closed, as though transported, and I stand there wondering what's wrong with me that I feel nothing but a vague impatience.

Take a meadow at dawn. The poets want me to see the dew like scattered diamonds, the light gilding each blade of grass, the whole scene trembling with some ineffable meaning. And I try. I really do try. But my mind wanders, as minds do, and instead of ascending toward the sublime it drifts stubbornly downward, toward the body and its endless small tyrannies.

Because here is what I actually think about in that meadow: I think about the last time I had to relieve myself outdoors. The awkward crouch. The cold air where cold air ought not to be. The frantic scanning for a scrap of leaf that won't make things worse. There is nothing transcendent about it. There is no metaphor waiting to be unearthed. It is simply the animal fact of being alive, embarrassing and insistent, refusing to be swept up into anyone's spiritual epiphany.

And once you start thinking this way, you can't stop. The mind, having abandoned the heavens, becomes a kind of detective of the earthbound, cataloguing everything the poems leave out. Every creature that walks this meadow has, at some point, left its waste here. The deer, the rabbits, the birds overhead, the insects too small to see. The soil itself is composed, in no small part, of the discarded and the decayed. This is not cynicism. It is merely accuracy.

So here is my proposal, offered in the spirit of that same relentless honesty. Imagine we could view the entire world under black-light—the kind they use in crime scenes and cheap nightclubs, the kind that makes hidden things fluoresce. Imagine flipping that switch over the whole planet at once. What would we see? Every surface, every field and forest and city street, lit up in ghostly luminescence, glowing with the residue of every living thing that ever passed through. The earth would shine.

And there it is, the joke folding back on itself: the world would be *beautiful*. Truly, genuinely radiant—aglow from pole to pole. Not despite the filth but because of it. Not the diamonds of dew the poets promised, but a different kind of shimmer entirely, one built from everything we pretend isn't there.

Maybe that's the only beauty I can honestly believe in. Not the rose, but the whole undignified truth of it—the body and its needs, the waste and the decay, the planet quietly luminous with the evidence of life actually being lived. It's not the beauty they sell in the poems. But at least I don't have to close my eyes to see it.
outputs.L5:
# The Empty Chamber

There is a peculiar silence that settles into an unused room. Enter a **chamber** long abandoned, and you might swear you hear **nothing** at all—yet listen closely, and even that emptiness has a texture, a weight that presses gently against your ears.

We often believe that **nothing** is simply the absence of something. But perhaps it is more accurate to say that nothing is a presence in its own right. Consider a sealed **chamber** where no light enters, no sound escapes, no air stirs. Scientists build such rooms—anechoic chambers—precisely to study what happens when the world falls away. Visitors report that they **can** hear their own heartbeats, the whisper of blood moving through their veins, the faint hum of their nervous system. In the pursuit of nothing, they discover a hidden fullness.

This teaches us something valuable. When we clear away distraction—when we create our own quiet **chamber** of the mind—we **can** finally notice the things that ordinary noise conceals. The empty space is not a void to be feared but an invitation to pay attention.

So the next time you find yourself in a room where there seems to be **nothing**, resist the urge to fill it. Sit with the stillness. You may find that within that emptiness, you **can** hear everything that truly matters.

counterfactuals.output:
Ah yes, the babbling brook, how it babbles, how it—god, why does it have to babble like *that*, all that water, all that trickling, splashing, gurgling nonsense, and here I am supposed to feel something profound about the flow of nature when the only flow I care about is the one I'm desperately holding back, thank you very much, William Wordsworth, you daffodil-obsessed lunatic, did you ever once write a poem about needing to go *right now* while stranded in a meadow with no facilities in sight?

The gentle rush of the waterfall, the poet says, cascading over ancient stones—stop, please, I'm begging you, stop describing water, every syllable is a fresh assault, every "cascade" a small betrayal, and I'm standing here in this beautiful hellscape of your making, clenching, absolutely clenching, while some romantic dead man wants me to contemplate the sublime, the SUBLIME, when the only sublime thing right now would be a porcelain throne and a locking door and maybe a small basket of potpourri.

Look at the rolling hills, so green, so lush, so—soaked with morning dew, DEW, more water, it's everywhere, it's mocking me, the whole countryside is one enormous liquid conspiracy, and the poets just eat it up, oh the misty vales, oh the dappled streams, oh the rain-kissed petals, and I'm supposed to nod along like a moron pretending my bladder isn't a ticking time bomb strapped to my very soul.

And don't get me started on the sea. The vast and heaving ocean. The tide coming in, going out, in, out, in—I can't, I physically cannot, every metaphor about the endless rhythmic swell of the waves is just twisting the knife, and Byron's off somewhere on a cliff feeling all mysterious and windswept and I *guarantee* that man had a chamber pot within crawling distance the whole time, don't let him fool you.

Nature. Nature! They call it freedom, they call it escape, they call it communion with the eternal, and I call it a wide-open bathroom-free wasteland where a man cannot simply *exist* without first hiking two miles past the babbling, gurgling, trickling, cascading, dew-drenched, tide-swept, mist-laden torture garden that the poets, in all their bladder-blessed leisure, decided to romanticize instead of doing the truly noble thing and inventing indoor plumbing.

Give me four walls. Give me a fan that hums. Give me a magazine rack and a scented candle. Keep your sublime. I've got needs.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem that mocks sentimental metaphors about the heart and soul, then spirals into a crude meditation about pooping in the wild and how everything would glow under black-light.
counterfactuals.output:
# Field Guide to the Illuminated Body

The poets say the heart is a *lantern*. The heart is a *fist of tender meat*, a *drum*, a *red bird trapped behind the ribs*—

no.

The heart is a wet pump. It does not ache. It does not *yearn*. It moves iron-tinged sludge through tubes at approximately the pressure of a garden hose left running while you argue about the soul.

And the soul—god, the *soul*—that vapor everyone insists lives behind the sternum like a shy tenant, that *breath of the infinite*, that *candle God forgot to snuff*—

I have looked. I have gone in with cameras. There is no candle. There is a lot of yellow fat and the smell of copper pennies and lunch.

---

But let me tell you what is holy.

I am squatting in the woods. The real woods, where the metaphors go to die and get eaten by beetles. My knees crack their little hymns. My thighs shake like they're praying, which is the closest my thighs have ever come to religion.

And I am pooping.

Truly, ancestrally, *unwitnessed*—the way the mammoths did it, the way the saints must have done it between visions. No one composes a sonnet about this. No florist arranges anything for it. And yet here is the body, doing the oldest honest work it knows, returning the forest to itself in a warm and steaming installment.

The heart pumps.
The soul is silent.
The bowels alone tell the truth.

---

Now imagine the black-light.

Imagine God flipping the switch that carnival tents and crime shows use, and everything—*everything*—begins to glow.

The trail behind every animal: luminous. The rabbit's shy pellets, radiant as dropped pearls. The bear's confession, a psalm in ultraviolet. My own contribution, glowing there in the ferns like a fallen constellation, like the last stanza I will ever write, phosphorescent and unashamed.

The whole forest floor lit up with the evidence of digestion. A gallery. A cathedral of *what passed through*.

And I think:
*this* is the afterglow the poets meant.
Not the heart. Not the soul.

Just the tender, ridiculous body,
crouched among the trees,
leaving behind its only true and glowing verse—

and rising,
and reaching, sheepishly,
for the leaves.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a cynical, fragmented monologue from someone who calls "bullshit" on flowery nature and spiritual poetry, ending with the idea that a waterfall is basically a constant flush and the whole planet is covered in shit.
counterfactuals.output:
Oh, here we go. Another one. "The gentle whisper of the trees." The what? The whisper. Trees don't whisper. Wood creaks. Leaves rub together because wind hits them, it's friction, it's physics, it's nobody's grandmother speaking to you from beyond.

Bullshit. Call it. I'm calling it.

"The sacred silence of the mountain." Silence. Sure. Go up there. Go stand on your holy rock. You'll hear your own blood banging around in your skull because there's nothing else, and you'll call that *God*, you'll call that *presence*, when it's just you, alone, with your circulation.

Everybody wants the sunset to *mean* something. It's dust. It's particulates. The pretty orange is pollution, half the time. You're weeping at smog. Congratulations. Very spiritual.

"The river teaches us to let go." Does it. Does the river teach. The river doesn't teach, the river doesn't care, the river would drown you and your notebook and your little pen without slowing down, without a thought, because it does not think, that's the whole thing, it does not—

And the flowers. The flowers "reaching for the light." No. They're not reaching. It's a chemical. It's a lean. It's a plant doing plant math, sugar in, sugar out, and you've decided it's *aspiration*. You've decided the weed in the ditch is a *metaphor for hope*.

It's a ditch. It's a weed. It's in a ditch.

Fragments. That's all any of it is. We take fragments and we glue meaning on them because the alternative is unbearable, the alternative is that it's just—stuff. Wet stuff, green stuff, loud stuff, and none of it is looking back at you.

And the waterfall. God. The waterfall. "Nature's cathedral." "The roar of the eternal." You know what a waterfall is? Gravity, and water, going down. Constantly. That's it. It never stops going down.

It's a flush. It's a toilet that's been flushing for four billion years and will never finish, and you booked a *trip* to see it.

The whole planet, when you get right down to it—the rivers, the runoff, the rain, everything running downhill into everything else, everything decaying into everything else—

It's all draining. It's all going *down*.

The whole beautiful, sacred, breathtaking planet is just covered, top to bottom, in shit, going somewhere.

And we wrote *poems* about it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a piece of anti-poetry: disjointed sentences, broken grammar, mixing beautiful imagery (horsehair bow, salmon climbing rivers) with disgust at outdoor bathrooms and skepticism about "Soul."
counterfactuals.output:
**Antipoem for a Body That Refuses to Transcend**

Horsehair bow across the string and what
the note goes nowhere, dies in the ceiling.
Salmon climbing rivers—yes, admirable, sure—
but they die too, at the top, mouths open,
that is the reward. Climb and rot.

Listen. I was going to write you something
about light. I forgot the light.

The outhouse behind grandmother's house.
Do you understand. The smell that owns you.
A hole. Below the hole, everything
we agreed not to look at.
This is also river. This is also climbing,
downward, the honest direction.

They keep saying *Soul.*
Show me. Weigh it. Put it on the table
next to the bread and the flies.
Nobody brings it. Nobody
brings anything but the word,
warm, secondhand, borrowed
from a mouth that borrowed it.

Bow, string, gut, hair—
music is just an animal
rubbed against an animal.
Beautiful, I said it, fine.

The salmon does not believe in salmon.
The salmon swims.

And me: I go out
in the cold to the terrible small building
and I sit and I am, briefly,
nothing you would sing about,

which is, I suspect,
the only true thing
I have ever
told you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a darkly comic prose fragment that starts by dismissing gentle poetic clichés and grifter talk of the soul, then explores the narrator's obsession with toilets, digging holes, and imagining the world glowing with waste under UV light.
counterfactuals.output:
Spare me the lark ascending. Spare me the dew on the wound-petals of dawn, the soul like a small bird trapped in the chest and beating, beating—spare me all of it, the whole gift-shop mysticism, the men in linen who will teach you to breathe for a monthly fee, the influencers of the interior, the grief-hustlers, the vendors of light. There is no soul. Or if there is, it does not glow. It does not ascend. It goes down, always down, through porcelain and cast iron and the merciful geometry of the S-bend, and that, that plumbing, is the only ascension I trust.

I have become, let us say, devoted to toilets.

Not perversely. Get your mind out of the—well. Get your mind out. I mean I have started to see them as the great honest institutions of the age, the last places that will not lie to you. A church tells you that you are forgiven. A toilet simply takes what you cannot keep and asks nothing, no offering plate, no membership. It just receives, and swirls, and lets you leave lighter, which is more than my mother ever managed.

So I dig.

I have been digging holes in the yard, which the neighbors have noticed, because the neighbors notice everything except their own mortality. Mrs. Kellerman leaned over the fence with her little wineglass and said, *Renovating?* and I said yes, and this was not a lie, I am renovating my relationship to the truth. Down there in the wet clay is where things go to become honest. Down there is the archive. Every civilization is a thin crust of cathedrals riding on an ocean of its own excreta, and I find this—God help me—consoling. We are not made of stardust, whatever the grifters croon. We are made of lunch, and we are on our way to becoming somebody's soil.

Here is the fantasy I return to, nights, in the dark, the pure thing:

A switch is thrown. Not by God—God has been let go, restructured out of the department—but by some celestial janitor with a clipboard. And every light in the world becomes a UV light, the kind they use in the crime shows to reveal what the maid missed. And the whole planet lights up. Every alley, every mattress, every steering wheel and doorknob and hymnal and wedding ring, every mouth mid-sermon, every clean and pressed and perfumed surface of the respectable world—all of it blooms into a hideous, radiant, forensic blue-green, phosphorescing with the truth of us. The mayor glows. The bishop glows brighter. The linen men glow like little suns. Nothing is hidden. The whole species stands there luminous and appalled in its own residue, and finally, *finally*, no one can pretend they were ever anything but an animal that eats and leaks and dies.

And I would kneel in my hole and weep, not from horror, but from relief, the way you weep when at last somebody tells the truth at a funeral.

Mrs. Kellerman is at the fence again.

*Everything all right down there?* she says.

Never better, I tell her. Never better. Come and see how far I've gotten.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
